applicable_when: The kernel is a GEMM (M=490, N=160, K=832) with ALLOW_TF32=False, meaning tl.dot uses scalar FP32 FFMA instructions instead of Tensor Cores. On H200, FP32 Tensor Cores deliver 989 TFLOPS vs 67 TFLOPS scalar — a ~14.7x theoretical gap. Enabling TF32 (allow_tf32=True) routes tl.dot through Tensor Cores at ~8x the throughput. Additionally, BLOCK_K=128 with tiny BLOCK_M=32/BLOCK_N=32 tiles causes severe 12-way shared memory bank conflicts (77.78% excessive wavefronts, 70.88% speedup potential) and limits shared-memory occupancy to only 3 blocks/SM. Reducing BLOCK_K to 32 or 64 while increasing BLOCK_M/BLOCK_N to 64 will: (1) reduce shared memory footprint to allow more concurrent blocks, (2) eliminate bank conflicts by aligning access patterns, and (3) produce larger MMA tiles that Tensor Cores handle efficiently.

strategy_title: Hardcoded Tile Enlargement Causes Register Spill and Slowdown
strategy_description: Increasing BLOCK_M and BLOCK_N from 32 to 64 (while reducing BLOCK_K from 128 to 64) caused registers per thread to jump from 94 to 128 (the hardware maximum), indicating register pressure saturation. This tripled the executed instruction count (3.1M → 9.9M) and more than doubled kernel duration (49.79 µs → 106.66 µs), despite a modest improvement in warp cycles per issued instruction (7.32 → 4.94). The root cause is that larger 2D tiles require more live registers to hold the accumulator and index variables, and when the register file is exhausted the compiler spills to local memory, dramatically increasing instruction count and latency. Enlarging tile dimensions without autotuning or verifying register budget is an anti-pattern when registers per thread are already near the hardware limit.
slow_pseudocode:
BLOCK_M = 32
BLOCK_N = 32
BLOCK_K = 128
# registers_per_thread = 94, duration = 49.79 us
fast_pseudocode:
BLOCK_M = 64
BLOCK_N = 64
BLOCK_K = 64
# registers_per_thread = 128 (maxed out), duration = 106.66 us  <-- REGRESSION
applicable_when: Never apply this pattern. Hardcoded tile enlargement without register budget analysis causes regression when registers per thread are already high (>80).
do_not_apply_when: Registers per thread are already ≥80 and approaching the hardware maximum (128 on Hopper/Ampere). Increasing BLOCK_M or BLOCK_N in this regime will saturate the register file, cause spilling, and multiply instruction count. The correct fix for SharedMemoryConflicts + high register pressure is to use @triton.autotune to search the tile space, or to reduce BLOCK_K only (not increase BLOCK_M/BLOCK_N) to cut shared memory footprint without inflating register demand.
framework_notes: Triton: registers per thread is controlled implicitly by tile sizes and accumulator shape. BLOCK_M × BLOCK_N accumulator tiles directly consume registers. On Hopper (SM 9.0), max registers per thread is 128; hitting this limit causes compiler spilling. Use @triton.autotune with num_warps and num_stages sweep rather than hardcoding enlarged tiles.
